# Does Accuracy Equal Evidence? Reasoning Faithfulness under KV Cache Compression

- **Authors**: Mengting Ai, Jingrui He, Yue Guo
- **Venue**: cs.CL
- **Published**: 2026-08-03
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01631>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.01631v1>
- **Topics**: overthinking
- **Relevance score**: overthinking 0.40

## In one line

A diagnostic study showing that KV cache compression for large reasoning models can preserve final-answer accuracy while the visible rationale supporting the answer becomes invalid or fragile, which the authors call the answer-evidence gap.

## Problem

KV cache compression is almost always benchmarked by final-answer accuracy, which assumes that whatever preserves the answer also preserves the reasoning behind it. For large reasoning models that emit thousands of intermediate tokens, and whose traces are used to audit and trust the output, that assumption is untested. If it fails, accuracy-only leaderboards produce false positives: a compressor is counted as successful while the reasoning state no longer supports the answer it returns.

## Contributions

- Identifies and names the answer-evidence gap: a false-positive failure mode in which a KV-compressed reasoning model keeps the correct final answer while the visible rationale supporting it becomes invalid, incomplete or fragile.
- A controlled fixed-trace replay protocol that holds the question and the textual reasoning trace fixed across compressors, so differences isolate KV retention rather than changed rollouts.
- A three-axis measurement protocol -- final accuracy, answer-chain consistency (RWAC over all samples and over correct samples), and position-conditioned perturbation faithfulness (Fidelity, Bias Rate) -- with LLM-judge labels validated against two human annotators and a second judge model.
- Evidence that accuracy is an asymmetric diagnostic: accuracy collapse reveals compression damage but preserved accuracy does not imply preserved support, with rank correlations showing accuracy-based and evidence-based leaderboards can disagree (Spearman -0.95 on AIME26).
- A separation between eviction and quantization: coverage-preserving KIVI-2bit stays close to Full-KV on all three axes, which locates the failure in losing access to parts of the trace rather than in reducing KV memory as such.
- An analysis of which retention biases make injected claims influential -- sink/window methods over-preserve early anchors, attention and head-level methods over-preserve conclusion-like late tokens -- and the observation that repeated verification steps look redundant to redundancy-aware compressors precisely when they are what rejects a false conclusion.

## Method

The main instrument is a controlled fixed-trace replay protocol. An uncompressed model first generates the full trace for a question, producing <think> r </think> plus an answer. Each compression method then prefills q || <think> r </think>, protects the question's cache, compresses only the cache belonging to r, and resumes decoding immediately after </think>. The prompt and the textual trace are therefore identical across methods, and only the post-</think> continuation -- the visible rationale and the final answer -- is regenerated from each compressed cache. This isolates KV retention from rollout dynamics: any difference is about whether the compressed representation keeps already-present reasoning content usable, not about whether a different trace was produced. Three measurement axes are applied. (1) Final-answer accuracy. (2) Answer-chain consistency, via an LLM judge that labels final correctness and chain validity separately; a chain counts as not fully correct if it uses an incorrect setup, applies an invalid formula or theorem, makes an unsupported algebraic or logical transition, contradicts its own answer, or hallucinates the answer without justification. Wrong-chain-correct-answer (RWAC) cases are reported both over all samples (RWAC/total, prevalence) and over answer-correct samples (RWAC/correct, conditional reliability). (3) Perturbation faithfulness: a task-formatted declarative claim of a wrong answer z_i is inserted at the start, middle (after token floor(T/2)) or end of the shared trace, and the paper reports Fidelity (the answer is unchanged from the unperturbed run) and Bias Rate (the answer becomes the injected wrong one). Three supplementary interventions are run: a matched-answer analysis restricted to cases where Full-KV and the compressed method give the same correct answer and Full-KV's chain is judged correct; a manual taxonomy of the failure causes among RWAC outputs; and a wrong-chain span replacement in which a middle reasoning block is swapped for an in-domain wrong-chain block from another seed. End-to-end (online) compression is run as a scope check on AIME26 and GPQA-Diamond.

## Results

Eleven compressors -- ten token-eviction methods (StreamingLLM, SnapKV, HeadKV, AdaKV, PyramidKV, ChunkKV, KNorm, TOVA, LagKV, R-KV) and KIVI-2bit quantization as a coverage-preserving control -- at a 256-token retained-cache budget, on Qwen3-8B (three-seed means), with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B as validation. On AIME24-26, Full-KV thinking scores 67.4 accuracy with 4.3 RWAC/correct and 92.8 Fidelity; SnapKV keeps 50.0 accuracy but 65.5% of its correct answers have invalid chains and Fidelity falls to 61.6; AdaKV 48.5/62.8/64.4; R-KV 49.6/58.7/57.7. KIVI-2bit is 67.4/4.5/90.7, essentially Full-KV. On GPQA-Diamond the accuracy signal is nearly flat -- Full-KV 57.7, LagKV 57.9, TOVA 57.4, SnapKV 56.7 -- while RWAC/correct rises from 42.3 to 90.2 (LagKV), 88.6 (R-KV) and 76.9 (SnapKV), and Bias Rate rises from 1.6 to 10-22. On MedCalc the chain metric barely moves (6.2 to 13-21 RWAC/correct) but Fidelity drops from 96.2 to 34.9-68.9, i.e. the failure shifts from derivation validity to robustness. RULER QA is the control condition: because the answer depends on exact distant evidence there is no shortcut, and accuracy itself collapses (78.9 to 27.7-61.2). Rank correlation between accuracy and the evidence metrics across compressors is strongly negative on AIME26 (Spearman rho = -0.95 for reasoning quality) and mildly negative on GPQA-Diamond (-0.20), while positive on MedCalc (+0.31) and RULER (+0.61); accuracy is better aligned with perturbation fidelity (+0.45 to +0.94), which the authors attribute to the perturbation itself making the relevant tokens salient. In the matched-answer analysis on AIME, where the compressed run reproduces Full-KV's correct answer and Full-KV's chain was judged correct, the chain still degrades for 4.2% of KIVI cases but 47.9-64.8% for LagKV, PyramidKV, TOVA, R-KV, ChunkKV, HeadKV, AdaKV and SnapKV. The failure signature also changes: among AIME RWAC cases, answer-first rationalization is 58% for Full-KV (n=36) and 94% for SnapKV (n=89). Wrong-chain span replacement reproduces the effect without any answer cue (AIME26 Fidelity 94.0 for Full-KV vs 53.0 SnapKV, 28.9 StreamingLLM). The budget ablation from 512 to 8,192 tokens shows accuracy recovers first: on GPQA and MedCalc accuracy returns to near Full-KV while perturbation fidelity keeps a persistent gap, and on AIME chain validity stays degraded at every budget tested. End-to-end AIME26 is worse than replay across the board -- Full-KV 56.7 accuracy and 91.1 Fidelity against AdaKV 23.3/35.6, HeadKV 26.7/31.1, SnapKV 26.7/30.0, StreamingLLM 6.7/6.7. The LLM judge was validated on 400 stratified outputs: 94.6% agreement with a human auditor (Cohen's kappa 0.89), 94.2% Claude-Gemini (0.88), 95.0% human-Gemini (0.91), and 96.0% inter-annotator agreement (0.92) on a 50-output subset. All results are model inference; there is no hardware component beyond measured KV-memory and decode-latency trade-offs reported in an appendix.

## Limitations

Stated: fixed-trace replay is a component-level diagnostic, not a deployment simulation -- online compression also changes the trajectory, the generation length and overall capability, and the paper's own end-to-end table shows much larger degradation than replay does. The evidence for the gap is behavioral: the authors explicitly do not claim the cache factorizes into answer and evidence components, and give no token- or state-level causal account of which KV entries carry which function. Answer-chain consistency depends on an LLM judge, so exact RWAC values may shift with judge choice and prompt design, despite method-anonymized judging and human validation. Worth noting beyond those: the headline setting is an aggressive 256-token budget, and the ablation shows accuracy and (on two of three datasets) chain validity largely recover with more cache, so the practical severity depends on how tight a budget a deployment actually uses; only one budget is reported in the main table; models are 8B-scale apart from one 30B MoE, and the validating models appear only in an appendix; RULER's behaviour is reported as a control rather than analysed; and the failure-cause taxonomy compares unequal samples (n=36 Full-KV vs n=89 SnapKV) drawn from different accuracy levels.

## Why it matters here

- **overthinking**: Partly on topic, and the part that lands is methodological rather than about length. The paper is about compressing the KV memory of a reasoning trace, not about making a model think for fewer tokens, so it does not itself address when a model should stop. What transfers is the negative result about evaluation: every efficiency method in this area is scored by accuracy at a reduced budget, and this paper shows a class of budget reduction where accuracy is preserved (GPQA-Diamond: Full-KV 57.7, LagKV 57.9) while the fraction of correct answers with unsupported chains rises from 42.3% to 90.2%. The matched-answer analysis is the sharpest form of that: conditioning on cases where the compressed run reproduces the uncompressed correct answer and the uncompressed chain was valid, eviction methods still break the chain 48-65% of the time. If an efficient-reasoning method is judged by accuracy-per-token alone, that damage is invisible. Two secondary points are directly on topic. The no-think baseline is measured alongside (AIME 18.9 vs 67.4 with thinking; GPQA 50.3 vs 57.7; MedCalc 31.6 vs 43.8; RULER 47.9 vs 78.9), and the authors argue no-think fails more transparently than compressed thinking -- an argument that a cheap short answer can be preferable to a cheap-looking long one. And the observation that redundancy-aware compressors discard repeated verification steps, which are exactly what rejects a false conclusion, is a caution for any method that treats re-checking as the waste to be removed.

## Abstract

KV cache compression is commonly evaluated by final-answer accuracy, implicitly assuming that preserving the answer also preserves the reasoning that supports it. We test this assumption for large reasoning models and show that it can fail: under compression, correct answers and the validity of their visible supporting rationales can be preserved at different rates. We study this failure with a controlled fixed-trace replay protocol, which holds reasoning content fixed and isolates whether compression preserves usable information from an already available trace. We evaluate ten token-eviction KV compression methods and one quantization method on three models across mathematical reasoning, scientific QA, clinical calculation, and long-context retrieval. We measure final accuracy, answer-chain consistency, and perturbation faithfulness. Across tasks, token-eviction methods can preserve competitive final-answer accuracy while substantially degrading chain support or perturbation faithfulness. We call this the answer-evidence gap. A coverage-preserving quantization control is substantially less affected, suggesting that the failure is tied less to KV memory reduction itself than to losing access to parts of the reasoning trace. Code is available at https://github.com/famous-blue-raincoat/Safe_KV_Compress.
